definition: Surfeit means an overabundant supply — too much of something, to the point of harm.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word surfeit. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know surfeit should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: A surfeit of trophies from the participation era filled four boxes that no one would ever unpack.
Sufficiency stops short of surfeit — a sufficiency is exactly enough, the point where a wise eater puts down the fork.
Excess stops short of surfeit — excess is more than needed, while a surfeit is excess arrived at the point of harm, the extra course you regret.

A surplus is the extra left over once needs are met — grain in the silo, budget carried forward — and it sits harmlessly in storage, often welcome. A surfeit is oversupply that has turned on its owner: whatever holds it, a market or a stomach, is already suffering.

Overindulgence is too much taken by choice — the fourth dessert, the extra hour of scrolling — excess a person consumes. Surfeit covers the whole territory of harmful too-much, including oversupply nobody chose: a surfeit can hurt a seller who never consumed a thing.

Surfeit means an overabundant supply — too much of something, to the point of harm.
The aid warehouse learned that a surfeit can paralyze as surely as a shortage: donated coats arrived by the ton after the telethon, and sorting them swallowed the volunteers' whole winter.

Surfeit is the abundance word with a stomachache built in — from an Old French verb meaning 'overdo.' A surplus sits harmlessly in storage; a surfeit has already been forced on someone, and the system — a market, a schedule, a digestion — is suffering for it.

Of this unit's abundance nouns, surfeit is the one that hurts: plenitude enjoys the fullness, plethora grumbles at the clutter, and surfeit pays for the excess — in stale markets, stuffed guests, or wasted winters.
Shakespeare's characters sicken from surfeits; keep the word for abundance with consequences.

When the harvest festival was canceled, three farms donated their entire pumpkin crop to the Riverside food bank in a single week.
The gesture was kind; the arithmetic was not.
The pantry could move perhaps two hundred pumpkins.
It received four thousand.
Volunteers stacked them in the hallway, then the parking lot.
Within days the surfeit became a problem of its own: crates blocked the loading dock, and the first pallets began to rot.
'Enough would have been a blessing,' the coordinator said.
'This much is a burden.' In the end the food bank paid a hauler to take half the crop away — spending money it had meant for groceries.
